Samsung X5 External SSD Thunderbolt 3 (500 GB)
This drive is marketed as the fastest External SSD currently on the market. From my testing they are not overstating that claim. I was able to transfer 250Gig of data (using a 2016 MacBook Pro) to the Samsung X5 drive in just over 7 minutes.

The drive uses a magnesium alloy (rather than aluminum) for this case. This means that the drive will not throw off as much heat. Due to this fact the drive has thermal management which will slow the drive down (after extended use) to keep it from over heating. Just be aware of this should you need to move very large files back and forth.

Pros
- Very fast transfer rates
- Comes with Thunderbolt 3 cable
- Solid build quality

Cons
- Expensive. The T5 version is only $109.00 [hence the one star drop. If a tad less expensive, we would have given it the full five stars.]
- Drive may slow down when continually transferring large files due to thermal management.
- Only works with Thunderbolt 3 ports.

review_title: Good Improvements Over Older Smart Watch Models
review_text:
I have used smart watches for a while now and I have seen a steady progression in the technology. This is my first Gen 6 watch. It is a big improvement from what I have used before (beyond just battery life) and so far I am pleased with it.

This is an Android-based smart watch, and it is similar in interface to previous smart watches I have seen and used. If you have used any generation of smart watch before this one the experience is very similar. I won't get too deep into the nuts and bolts of that or the WearOS app.

There are two big areas of improvement I have seen with this new watch. First, the battery life is much better than previous smart watches I have used which is very encouraging. I have a Gen 2 watch that I love but it lasts only about 3 days on a charge, and my Gen 5 is not much better. This one lasts several days before the battery runs out.

The more important improvement to me, though, is the way it doesn't interfere with the Bluetooth in my car. Previous watches messed up my ability to stream to the car's sound system to the point that the sound would sputter and simply die. I did trace it to the watch by powering off the watch completely after which the problem went away and would come back when the watch was powered on. This watch does not interfere at all and my car's Bluetooth works whether the watch is on or not.

This is a stylish watch, a bit more upscale than some of the others I have seen and used. The band is a non-stretch link band that is a little snug but not unworkable.

So far this watch works well for me. I am pleased with the improved battery life and even more happy that it doesn't mess with my car's Bluetooth connectivity.

review_title: Works with Linux; Small and Fast
review_text:
Crucial is one of the first names that comes to mind when I have needed reliable RAM for my systems in the past. I have a Crucial 500MB SSD in one of my systems and it has served me well over the years so I was interested in this SSD as a back-up option for pictures and data. It has proven to be a fine solution for my needs.

Right up front – yes, it works with Linux right out of the box. I plugged it into my Peppermint Linux system and the kernel immediately recognized the drive and made it available. It was on me to mount the drive, but this was a simple matter and I was able to access the file system and see drive statistics. Obviously it works with Windows so I won’t go into that.

This is a physically small device, slightly less than half the size of a cell phone (iPhone 6s is what I used for comparison). It will easily fit inside the change pocket in my jeans and can tuck just about anywhere. This is a double-edged sword. On one hand it is convenient to have something this small and easy to store, but it is also easy to misplace or even lose. If this stays in your laptop bag or briefcase it should be secure, but if you are in a habit of keeping things in your pockets instead be cautious.

Transfer speeds are good. I have not done benchmarks on this drive but I copied thousands of pictures (average size about 8mb per file, some more and some less) and it was significantly faster than the USB drive I have been using for a while and faster than many of the thumb drives I have been using for backups. I have no complaints.

This is a small and fast drive that just works. It works with Linux which for me is important, and it is small enough to tuck in my camera bag for making backups in the field.

review_title: Solid Performance; Slightly Pricier than Competitors
review_text:
I have built systems with SSDs for the last several years and I have come to see where they have their strengths and weaknesses. Not all SSDs are the same, and some have distinct advantages over others though the gap is definitely narrowing. This is my first experience with Samsung’s SSDs, and so far it has been a very positive experience. It has given me no issues at all and has performed well.

I installed the drive in a Dell Inspiron laptop which was running Windows 8. On the SSD, I installed Linux instead. Installation was very smooth, it was quick and I had a working system up and running in no time. I have now been running the system constantly for over a week (no powering off or hibernating) and the drive has shown no signs of trouble.

I loaded up a virtual machine and ran it on top of the main installation. The VM and the host install both have performed admirably and have not suffered from any noticeable I/O lag. Running smartctl against the drive after the past week of testing, it has reported no errors and a very healthy drive across the board.

Aside from the speed advantages of an SSD over a platter-based drive, this drive is absolutely silent (no surprise there) and so far I have not had any heat issues. It has given me no indications of any trouble in operation and my system is running as smoothly as should be expected.

The one issue I have with this drive, and it’s not a performance or quality issue, is the pricing. It is a little more expensive than most, and so far I have not seen any real justification for it over the likes of Crucial, Kingston or other branded drives. There may be justifiable reasons that reveal themselves later (I do not know how long this drive will continue to work but it should literally last for several years, even under very heavy use), but for now it seems a tad expensive compared to competitors.

Operationally I cannot find fault with this drive. It works well, it’s fast and quiet (as should be expected) and so far I’ve not had heat issues with it. Utilities I have run against it have shown that the drive is very healthy and has reported no problems out of the box. This is a good drive that will serve well. Time will tell, though, if it is worth the slightly higher asking price.

review_title: Fast, Quiet, and Works Great Under Windows and Linux
review_text:
NOTE: I am writing this review for the 1TB platter-based Passport drive.

I have a 250GB Passport I bought several years ago and it has served me well, though it has gotten close to full over time (I never imagined at the time that I would fill that thing up). I have had good fortune with it so I expected the same from this 1TB version, and so far I have been right. In addition to the larger capacity, it is very definitely a speed upgrade from my old Passport.

This is a small drive in terms of physical footprint, approximately 4”x3”x0.5” in dimension. That’s a double-edged sword. On one hand, it is small enough to stuff in a shirt pocket which makes it an excellent on-the-go storage solution that’s almost as convenient as a thumb drive. But, that also means it is easy to misplace or lose (or have stolen if left unattended).

It comes with software that allows you to password-protect the drive which is a nice deterrent in the event that the drive is taken. It’s certainly not foolproof, but it’s sufficient to keep the large majority of unauthorized access out. To be honest, since the drive does not leave my home I have not used the software at all.

When you plug in the drive to a Windows or Linux system, the OS immediately recognizes the drive and it is available immediately for use. In the case of Windows, you can immediately explore the drive and read from it and write to it. For Linux, it depends on how you have configured automount and which desktop management software you use, but the kernel does register the presence of the drive and you can display the partition table.

This is a USB 3.0 drive, making it a huge speed upgrade from my older 2.0-based Passport. This is a great solution for storing all of your pictures, movies, important documents, and as in my case large downloads and purchased software packages. With 1TB of space, I don’t think I am going to run out of space anytime soon.

As a bonus, this is a very quiet drive.

I put this drive on a USB power meter to see how much it draws from the USB port. At rest it pulls 0.17A. When actively reading, it peaks just under 0.6A which is surprisingly low. My concern was that this would add some strain on the USB port over a longer period of time but this seems to be an unjustified concern. That said, I am more likely to connect it to a USB hub instead of directly to a USB port.

So far I have no complaints with this drive. It’s a big step up for me from my older Passport, being larger, faster and more quiet. It’s not cost prohibitive either which is just a bonus. If you need a decent backup drive with large capacity and a small footprint, this one is worth consideration.

review_title: Good NAS Drive; Can Work in USB Enclosure with Some Effort
review_text:
A NAS is a great way to add storage for the whole network where everything can be reached from any system connected. It is not as simple as a USB mass storage device like a thumb drive, of course, but it addresses a completely different issue. So far, this drive has proven to be a good one, though its reliability remains to be demonstrated over the long haul.

I have the 8TB drive, and it is great for dumping huge numbers of videos, music, documents and other media needed across a small network. It is fairly fast too, so streaming video from the NAS to any given device on the network is reasonably smooth as long as the network can handle the bandwidth (keep this detail in mind if you are wanting to stream video over a slower wireless network - the lag isn’t necessarily the drive’s fault). The drive is very quiet, though not silent, and so far seems to stay acceptably cool.

I did learn that it does not work all that well in a USB drive enclosure right out of the packaging. I have an enclosure that is capable of handling drives up to 8TB so I decided to try an experiment with the drive when it first arrived. I put it in the enclosure and connected it to my Windows 10 laptop. The system saw the device, and it even saw the drive and recognized the model and serial number, but it was unable to access the drive or even format it. I had more success with my Linux system which recognized the drive and was able to access the partition table and display drive parameters. I did not repartition the drive or create a file system for my experiment though I believe it would have worked.

Time will tell if this drive will be reliable over the long haul. Based on my experience so far, it has worked out well and I have had no issues. It’s the largest drive I have worked with and can handle a LOT of data. If you need wide open spaces for your network storage solution (or you are willing to fiddle with it to get it working as a USB solution) this is a good choice.

It comes in 3 boxes and the boxes will be delivered to the room of your choice. You need to attach the backs and the cushions get zippered together and Velcro into place. The couch looks nice and is comfortable to sit on. Not sure how long it will last but for the price it meets our needs.

review_text:

I'm very happy with the Fitdock app. No weird translation issues like with other apps I've tried. It's easy to understand, and it works well. It's fun to be able to use a picture from my phone as the background screen on my watch. The silent alarm works well too, it wakes me without waking my spouse, a great feature when couples are on different work schedules.

A couple of features I wish the smart watch had- the ability to monitor blood pressure (though I know it's not really a medically approved method), and a reminder to drink water. But these don't really detract from how nice this watch is, so I didn't remove any stars for it. I think this smart watch would make a great gift for someone who is interested in smart watches, but concerned about paying the high price for the brand name models.

review_title: Great for computer backup, digital photos & videos
review_text: I have two of the Seagate 1TB external hard drives (one for me, one for my husband). We've been extremely happy with them so I was eager to try out the 5TB. I stored copies of all the photos I have from over the last two decades, family videos, scanned copies of important documents & files. It's amazing how much the drive can store. It doesn't bother me that it has to be powered by an ac adapter because I have it connected to my desktop computer. File transfer is fast, and luckily I've had no issues with heat. However, I still make sure nothing falls on or covers any part of the drive, just in case. I think it's a great drive for the price.

Update: I see a lot of people complaining about the drive capacity being “wrong” (465gb instead of 500gb or 960gb instead of 1TB) and to those people I highly recommend going to YouTube and searching “What is Overprovisioning?” and clicking on the link by TechQuickie.

Samsung is NOT falsely advertising. The drive DOES in fact come with the advertised space it’s just that in order for it to work properly and perform optimally it requires approximately 10% of the capacity to be overprovisioned free space.

This is a really great SATA SSD for the price. It's perfect for storing games that have long load times without paying a fortune for an NVMe SSD of equal capacity. I highly recommend it for people like me who need more space for games, projects, and other things like that who want them to load quickly. You can get an HDD like a WD Black for cheaper but the loading times will be much longer and for those who dont like to wait for long load screens this is a perfect choice.

Also don't forget to enable RAPID mode. It uses RAM to speed up the programs & applications that you have been using recently. My CrystalDisk benchmark shows how fast it is with RAPID mode enabled.

review_title: Monitor Your Home or Office with Ease but try to Ignore the Wires
review_text:
Q- see 12 camera security system is a nice way to protect a home or business from threats. Install the cameras in different sections of the home or company and then access from home, online, etc. for top level security.

This security system seems much more complicated than it really is and the reason, I think, is due to the number of cameras. Looking at all of those cameras, out of the box, is a little bit intimidating and it leads one to believe that setup will take days and even weeks to complete. But it is actually much simpler than it looks and there is no need to install all 12. Just use the number of cameras you feel is necessary and store the rest for later use.

With this security system in place, you can access the live feed through the internet and even on your mobile phone via the Q- See applications. This is great for convenience and its one of the security systems best features. Other security systems have this feature as well, so it’s nothing unique. But it is very easy to use and it lets you monitor specific places on a property, for maximum security. Wherever you might be, home or away, you can take a look at what’s going on by pulling the mobile phone from your pocket. It doesn’t get much easier than that.

The one issue I have with this system is the same one others have complained about, and that is the wires. In the modern world in which we live, we expect wireless technology more and more. This system is wired and it could present some problems as you try to tape wires and otherwise conceal them from view. If this was a wireless system and I could place the cameras anyplace I like, then I would be hard pressed to find much wrong with this product. But I know many people who would likely reject this product immediately for this reason alone.

Security is important, especially for those who live in less safe areas or who operate a small business in a vulnerable area. With Q- See watching the home or business, you can feel a little more at ease. The cameras detect motion and can quickly help you catch a person in the act of theft, trespassing, or vandalism, providing proof positive of what happened and where. Like I said, the lack of wireless technology is a problem but if you can get past that issue, you will find that this is a very good security system for home or business needs.

review_title: Installation of the Corsair H80i V2 wasn't easy in this smallish case but the radiator sandwiched between ...
review_text:
I received this cooler today and installed it along with two new 140mm front panel case fans.
I have an AMD based system running stock cooling that came with the case and hardware components.
My system temps running stock cooling were way to high, idyling at temps around 45c to 50c and when running
demanding applications temps would shoot way up into the 80's and 90's sometimes causing shutdowns.
I kept remembering statements from AMD advising consumers to keep the down blowing fans installed but I decided
to try a liquid cooling solution out of desperation.

My case is a Corsair Spec 02.
My motherboard is a Asus Sabertooth 990FX R2.0.
The processor is a AMD FX-8320.
The graphics processor is a Sapphire Radeon R9 380.
That AMD FX 8320 runs hot, extremely hot also the NB and SB components on the Asus MB run very hot.
My system temps were way to high, I had to do something.

Installation of the Corsair H80i V2 wasn't easy in this smallish case but the radiator sandwiched between
the two 120mm fans does fit in this case. I followed the manufacturer recommendation and configured both
fans to push air inward into the case. This case has perforated holes in the roof for ventilation and this
allows used air to evacuate out of the case assuming the fans are configured to blow inward which will push
air out those top vents.
The two big 140mm red LED fans I installed in the front panel are configured to pull air inward and I set them
to run at 100% speed (1000 RPM), they are Cougar Red LED's, very high quality fans that move a lot of air
silently.

This Corsair H80i V2 has got to be the best liquid cooler available for smaller cases like mine, it has dropped
my system temps by 20 to 30 degrees C instantly. I am seeing system temps lower than I've ever seen them since
I built the system back in December 2015.

This fridge is rocking my system. Cool is good, the cooler the better when it comes to computer systems. I have
Core Temp 1.0 RC6 installed and it is showing my CPU temps idling at 13C - 15C... That is chill.

Chill is good.

Thanks Corsair, this liquid cooler system is awesome.
Thanks Amazon for the excellent service and thanks UPS for being the most dependable carrier on earth.
My system purrs away at 15C, OMG this is awesome.

During the Covid Pandemic, all the regular brand name webcams were sold out so I found myself trying out a bunch of these no-name brands from Amazon. The last one I tried actually had a much harsher fisheye effect in the corners, as well as over-saturated color. This one seems far less cartoony and more realistic in color reproduction, as well as being somewhat more rectilinear (photo speak for straight lines being straight, not as much curved distortion). There is a bit of fisheye curve on the edges, but it is very usable and didn't make my ceiling look concave like my last one I tried. See attached images for examples of the room's wall distortion. It's there if you are looking for it, but not terrible when you're looking at a subject. The microphone is just meh. I have a desktop mic and the sound out of that was MUCH better, especially because you can get it closer to your face than the camera. But the fact that this HAS a mic is a good option in a pinch. I would just strongly recommend an external mic if you want people to hear you clearly. Also something I didn't know before trying this:
It is MANUAL focus! That means it won't follow and focus on you automatically, you have to twist the lens until you're sharp in the view. It actually isn't that hard to nail focus, the depth of focus is pretty deep so once you've set it for your standard sitting distance, you likely won't have to change it ever again unless you walk away from the camera. And, as you can see, the X5 is really fast. If you need speed and have Thunderbolt 3, this is a great drive.

Installation was easy. My Mac recognized the drive right away. I could've just used it, but Samsung provides a utility on the drive for enabling its onboard encryption and keeping its firmware up to data. Recommended.

(But do make sure your computer has Thunderbolt 3. You can't tell just by looking at the ports, as TB3 is implemented as a superset of USB-C. So, Thunderbolt 3 is USB-C but the converse is not true. Similarly, previous-rev Thunderbolt interfaces aren't forward-compatible to TB3 devices. Some of the one-star reviews of this drive are clearly from folks who didn't know these issues.)

review_title: Was A 1 Star Until I Adjusted It, Makes It 4 Stars
review_text:
I received this mouse on September 17th. It is now December 19th, so I have given it three months of use before writing this review. Before purchasing this 3M mouse, I was using just your average, typical, mouse with a scrolling wheel in the center. For work I am on the computer around 13 hours a day. Recently my right wrist, forearm, and shoulder started to ache and eventually became very painful because of the unnatural position my mouse held my hand/arm in. Also I use the scrolling wheel very often and my middle finger (which I used to scroll with), started to swell and experience pain in the joints, with a hard, painful bone-like spur on the underside.
After using the 3M Ergonomic mouse, the swelling/pain in my finger joint went away immediately, and the bone spur also dissipated.
However, while it did alleviate the pain in my wrist, it actually caused more pain in my forearm and shoulder, and now the bonus of the entire thumb area of the hand - from the wrist up to the tip of my thumb. After a week of looking at the design and messing around with folded towels under my arm, it finally dawned on me why this mouse caused so much pain....

Though I purchased the 'small', the hand shaft is still too long, and with the toggle button at the top of it, it holds the thumb in an unnatural upward position thereby putting strain on that entire bone. When you lay your arm down on a table, with palm facing inward, in the relaxed position a thumb is NOT sticking upwards, but instead it naturally lays level with the index finger. Hence the hand shaft is too tall.

The shaft cannot be cut down obviously, so the 'deck', the part that the hand rests upon, had to be raised. To to do this I took a few sheets of paper towels, folded them to the thickness that would give the best height for my hand, then wrapped sturdy packing tape around it, to keep it folded (and makes it easy to wipe clean). Then I made a 'collar' out of paper towel to go around the base of the hand shaft, to which I taped the front part of the folded paper towels to, it helps keep it from shifting. I then put a large piece of rolled tape on the rest of the 'deck' which holds the rest of the folded towels onto the deck.
Did it work?
Yes, it did. The paper towels have conformed perfectly to the shape of my hand, and is very comfortable. It stays rather clean because of being wrapped in packing tape, which I periodically wipe clean with rubbing alcohol. More importantly, it has elevated all pain in my arm, shoulder, and thumb area. It holds my hand and fingers in a very natural position.

So while it is not perfect, and I shouldn't have to make padding for it, I gave this mouse 4 stars because I do like it, even though I had to make adjustments to make it work. It glides smoothly on a mouse pad. The toggle button is smooth, as is the scroll button. It does take some time getting used to scrolling this way, but once I got the hang of it, it's second nature to me now.

Some tips:
* I found myself 'gripping' the mouse like a joy stick because I was so not used to a mouse of this shape, which makes the four fingers hurt after a while and would make me hit the scroll button inadvertently. I had to keep reminding myself to relax my hand. No need to 'grip' it, it's not going to take you on a 'white knuckle' ride!

* Does not move well on thin or hard surfaces. I had a very, very thin mouse pad and it would not glide well on it. I purchased a thicker pad and now it moves smoothly.

* Because the hand shaft stands so far up, I have knocked this mouse right off my desk a number of times, my arm would hit it, or walking past my desk my sweater would catch it. So when not in use keep it away from the edge of the desk. At least I know that this mouse can take a beating!

This monitor supports Freesync from 40-144Hz over both HDMI and DP with a recent AMD Graphics card. The newer NVIDIA cards also work fine using adaptive sync, but only over DP.

For the people who can't get 144 Hz on their AMD Graphics card, try going to Windows 10's "Display Settings" page, open Advanced display settings. Open Display adapter properties for your connected Display. Click on "List All Modes" and,using the drop-down menu, set your resolution/Refresh rate to "1920 by 1080, True Color (32 bit), 144Hertz". After that, you should be running at 144 Hz. Enable freesync in your monitor's OSD, then you should be able to enable freesync through AMD Radion Settings.

If using an NVIDIA card, it's much simpler. Use NVIDIA Control Panel's Display settings to change the resolution to 1920 x 1080 (native) under the PC header, setting the Refresh Rate to 144Hz. Enable Freesync on the Monitor's OSD, Then you can set up adaptic sync using Nvidia Control Panel/Display/Set up G-Sync.

At the end of the day, I'd end up purchasing the Samsung M8 for a few reasons.

I'm usually a WD fan, but the Samsung M8 is faster in most practical user situations. Most reviews will state the WD drive as being faster, but that is only with very large file copy sequences - writing/reading files in this way is not what most people want a drive for.

The Samsung M8 is zippier with practical file operation - such as flowing through large batches of music or photography. If you edit photographs, the Samsung will be faster. If you are moving large batches of HUGE files (such as ISO's, disc images, etc), the WD will be faster, but only by 3-4 MB/s. For how much faster the Samsung is in most areas (nearly double the speed, 40mb/s vs. 20mb/s), getting the Samsung is more practical.

The Samsung is almost double the speed of the WD with most file operation, such as editing photography or flowing through music.

I use this as the main OS disk in my build. It is faster than the SATA III stuff. It is hard for me to perceive the difference since we are talking about seconds, even if the difference is in several magnitudes. I bought this over the other SSD mainly due to longer life that comes from being MLC, rather than speed.

My drive idles at 45C and on writes the temperature goes up. I have installed an NVMe heatsink on it, the kind that wraps around (versus the kind that just glues to the top). This buys more time before thermal throttling hit due to temperature.

One thing to keep in mind is that the rated speeds that are posted on most gaming SSDs (at least with Samsung) are for burst writes. That speed drops significantly for sustained writes. Meaning large file copy operations will show slower overall speeds. You would need to buy Enterprise rated SSDs at x4 to x10 the price if that is what you need. With game loads you would want burst speeds anyway. The other problem with NVMe is that by being smaller it reduces how much heat they can dissipate, which also limits large file copy operations. It is an inherent limitation.

I had a smaller one in the past, but it filled up so fast with all the work I had to do in college, that it was about time I just got a new one for the real world now that I just graduated. I'm hoping this will last me a while. It came in beautiful packaging in a metal tin. This could easily be a great Christmas or graduation gift. I'll be getting another one for my older nephews soon as they start high school and college soon. If you have tons of photos or documents, this is for you!

I've looked at smart watches and balked at the price. It seemed too much money on something that I might not like or use much or for very long. The modest price on this one made me decide to try it out. I am glad that I did because I've been wearing it and using it for more than a month now.

Besides the obvious telling time function I've used the various functions on a regular basis, particularly the step counter and sleep tracker. The only problem I have had is that there really wasn't much in the way of instructions included with this so mostly I have been figuring this out by trial and error.

Overall I am pleased with this watch, and I am using it more than I thought I would. I would have preferred more written instructions with this so I could access the various functions without going through so much trial and error.

review_title: Different for an old time mouse user
review_text:
This was listed as wireless, but did not specify wifi. I assumed it was bluetooth. Even though I got this to use with my tablet, I ended up testing this on a desktop.

They do have laptop users in mind though. It is clever of them to use the battery compartment as a storage spot for the dongle. That defintely adds to its portability.

As for comfort and usage, I've used an actual three button mouse (no wheel) for decades at work. But using this at home was a non issue, minus the USB A dongle.

For me it was no more comfortable than using an old fashion mouse, but I've never had problems. So this ends up being just different.

review_title: Arrived bent with cross threaded bolts
review_text: Cheaply made. Also arrived damaged. Be prepared to have to go out to the store to buy new bolts in order to actually set it up.

review_title: Sound Okay - But Break Quickly (ASD Alert)
review_text:
My ASD kid has great ears and listens to music and videos and everything but his surroundings all day every day. It's a crucial coping skill for him. For years, we have bought the cheapest earbuds we can find, because he fidgets the cords and the break.

Most of the expensive earbuds do not sound much if any better than the cheap ones, but these KZ ZEX Pro buds DO sound noticeably better.

Unfortunately, they break just as fast. Like 3 pairs in 4 months fast. So, for now, we are back to the cheap ones.

For years running 16gb ram on a 2010 mini was a rumor: one you believed at risk of wasting a ton of money. My set up was good enough to run the old OS I was running, so I didn't press the issue. Than I ran into some issues where I needed to upgrade, and the ram and HDD were probably going to struggle.

So I got out the tiny screwdrivers.

This ram works perfectly. All recognized right out of the box with no issues - I put everything in at once (installed an SSD at the same time), did an internet OS install, and TA DA! Core2Duo is faster than a recent i3.

This is a very inexpensive curved screen monitor. Very inexpensive. It's being used for Pro Tools, and lag time is imperceptible. Resolution is fine. No problems. Works as well in this context as a much fancier model that is its partner in a dual screen set up.

However, the hubs was having issues with his bluetooth peripherals and web searching disclosed that curved monitors can interfere with the bluetooth. I don't pretend to understand how or why, but take away the monitor and the interference stops. For his needs, though, the monitor is more important than having wireless peripherals, so corded mouse and keyboard to the rescue.

Such an easy upgrade, I barely remember it. The kit comes with nice, sharp, magnetized tip versions of both of the screwdrivers you need. Presto change-o, no more "drive almost full" messages.

The drive seemed a little sluggish to start, but as soon as I repaired permissions, it was screaming fast. I put the kit in my wish list some time ago, and the price has come down by quite a lot. Right now, this kit and a used 64gb 2012 MBA make for my all time favorite Mac since my old SE.

review_title: terrible - dongle was bad and would have shorted my port out but not for autostop
review_text: Mine came with a bad USB dongle. When I say bad, I mean almost blew out my usb port bad. Cute little thing, but I threw it away.
Had this webcam before, cats chewed on the cord. The replacement is the same trusted webcam! I use it for working from home.
Plug the USB cord into a USB port, and you instantly have a working external hard drive. I use it to backup my entire internal hard drive.
My laptop has only 2 USB ports, and pretty much everyone could use more than 2 USB ports. The product works wonderfully!
This hybrid drive resurrected my old MacBook. It cut my start up time by around half. Thank you for great technology for a great price.

review_title: Slow and bogs down my wireless mouse.
review_text:
I don't know whats going on, but just got this and my transfer speeds at 3.0 was at 38mb and my whole computer started slowing down bogging my wireless mouse badly.
Now I don't have a antique computer, I have a I7-2600k with 16G ram
I stopped it and then restarted the transfers and the speed went up to 74mb now.
I know ext drives are not as fast on USB of course, but why is it killing my usb controls.
I use a trackball mouse by Logitech, and I had a movie running while playing a online game, normal stuff, but when this started transferring it slowed my controls down heavily.
Will give this a few days to see how it works as my media center, if it fails then back it goes and will try the notebook by WD and see if its better.
Excellent fast hard drive with tons of space!

My first external drive ever was a Western Digital so I have a soft spot for the brand. Since we needed to back up an older laptop that was starting to fail, this WD 4TB My Passport Ultra Portable External Hard Drive with USB appeared at a perfect time. It has two things that we need: ease of use and storage space. It was easy to use for back up of the laptop's data and had so much storage left that we could use it to transfer files from the other PCs. We still have a lot left for storage. We aren't a big cloud using family but I imagine if we were, we'd use it as a back up for the Cloud as well. Overall, it has worked out well for our household.

I have been looking for a quiet keyboard and this one fits the bill! I love the cover that comes with it since it makes it easy to clean and offers some extra protection. It's a great keyboard and I loved the reasonable price. Very happy!

One of the best wireless mice that I've used. It's cheap enough, it fits in the hand very well (I typically wear large or XL gloves), and it has a back and forward button on the side which is nice. Tracks on most surfaces, and the batteries last quite a while in it.

review_title: The new de facto modular psu
review_text: Great construction and quality overall. Great for your average pc. Couldn't ask for more especially for the price.

Due to COVID19, I am working from home on my laptop which was causing back/neck issues. So I ordered this monitor because it was the cheapest one and it had the HDMI cord included (those really were my only criteria). It arrived today, I unpacked the monitor and cables, plugged it into my laptop (a company issued hp Elitebook and BAM! it just worked. I am up and running, no problems. So for now - 5 stars. If anything changes, I will return to adjust my review. (I haven't used the speakers to know if they are good or bad, if I want to listen to something I will do so through my external speakers).
I have puchased seval of these over the years for clients and they are all still working. Clients like the way the look. I will buy more of them.

The change to this from a regular SSD feels similar in speed to the change to SSD from HDD. The boot drives in my next build will very likely be an m.2. The heat sink is a nice touch. Looks great, feels high quality, I'm not sure if it actually improves performance at any really level.
Seemed fine, it didn't work with the laptop that I ordered them for; but that was really my fault. I gave five stars because returning the product was pretty low hassle.
Works great. The software to customize the buttons is easy to use and the mouse is very comfortable in my hand. No complaints at all

review_title: It's so obvious that there weren't too much thinking went to making this thing
review_text: It may be great for laptops but I'm using this for a desktop. The frame is almost half the size of the space of a regular slim dvd drive. The holes to screw the caddy tight into place are a little small. I had to find a different screw. Oh, the product doesn't come with screws for the outer frame. I have had to return this particular motherboard a total of four times already and each time for different reason. It will work for like a day or two then your system will then gives you the Blue Screen of death or a SATA port would drop the drive or the anyone of the memory banks would fail out of nowhere. Avoid this board and the brand as much as possible. ASUS customer service phone line is the worst. Expect no pickup or wait a really long time to get to a live person. One of the best decision when it comes to savings. It has plenty of SATA & IDE power cables. Have been using it for two months and nothing bad happened so far. Plus it's cheap so you can always get another one.
Works good right out of the box.

Like others have already said before me, this is a very comfortable mouse, being that is is larger than most mobile mice by comparison. The Rubber curved sides and arching top molds to the hand's natural resting position, so that it is pretty ergonomic for a mobile mouse. I am able to use the mouse on wood, cloth, and about most flat surfaces. I am overall happy with this purchase

review_title: We use this at work to back up photos and ...
review_text: We use this at work to back up photos and video. We also have online backups and network backups, but we go one step farther with our digital media.

These are the best monitors (I use 2) I have ever had so far, and the price was simply crazy low. The colors are great and identical on both monitors. In my case, my gpu only had 1 DVI out but had multiple display output ports and 1 HDMI out. I thought the second monitor attached via an HDMI cable was at first showing muted colors, until I played with the driver UI. After getting frustrated having to reset the colors after every screen reset, I got the idea of using the included HDMI-to-DVI converter that came with the monitor. That worked like a charm. So I have the second monitor hooked up from the GPU using HDMI out then going through the HDMI-to-DVI converter and into the monitor. For whatever reason HDMI sucks. I don't use the built in speakers on the monitor so I don't miss it and now I don't have to worry about resetting colors.
Maybe the 980 is better, but this card just works supremely and is very cool.

review_title: Fortunately it fits just barely in my Sentey Gaming case
review_text:
Boy is this big. Fortunately it fits just barely in my Sentey Gaming case. I had purchased the Arctic Freezer 7 Pro Rev 2 but that was far worse than the AMD 8350's included cooler fan, probably because the contact surface is designed for Intel chips and is much smaller than for AMD chips.
Be prepared for some work installing this fan as you have to install a new back-plate on the motherboard. The included parts are perfect in that they provide everything you will need including the thermal compound. So I also purchased the 2 top case fans (Corsair series). Without the cooler, the top fans did indeed reduce the top CPU temperatures by about 4C degrees - almost as though the case cover is open. With the cooler though the CPU temperature never climbed beyond 61C degrees even when all 8 cores were saturated (was compiling code). Without the cooler and the the top fans I was hitting 70C degrees which is 5 degrees above allowed operating temperature. I am surprised my AMD 8350 is still operational. With the cooler and top fans the temperature drop is 15C which is a win! Maybe I can use the Arcrtic Freezer in an Intel setup.

review_title: Top end in airflow, great looks, and quality materials. Buy it!
review_text:
[[VIDEOID:8957394ebc48aefec4c186a67e317914]] Wonderful case which blew away my expectations. I moved all my components to this one from the CoolerMaster Q300L, which looked and felt cheap and was very loud with the 5 fans I put in to help with temperatures. I knew that heat at some level hurt performance, but I had no clue how much my own rig was being crippled by it until I got this. I've been able to significantly move up my graphics settings in Witcher 3, Battlefield V, and Shadow of The Tomb Raider, and my framerates are still higher and more stable than they used to be. It feels more as if I upgraded my gpu than anything I imagined a case being able to improve on its own (I have a 1070 Ti btw). If you have a case with poor or mediocre airflow stop reading and buy this! (Youtube reviewers rank it at or near the top of everything in the market when it comes to this).

It doesn't hurt that it looks fly as hell. Putting in a vertical gpu adapter was a breeze as it required no modding or hassle whatsoever to install in this case(the sound in the video comes from a ceiling fan in the room btw). More than satisfied, I am thrilled with the H500

I didn't have too much sag in my new build to start with, but wanted the peace of mind of not having any unnecessary stress pulling on my PCIe slot over the years. With this support system I was able to very easily secure my gpu at the precise angle I wanted. The materials feel very high grade and sturdy, and it looks great inside my pc. Even the packaging is crazy high end for a ~$10 - $15 part.

Also, I have my power supply and a fan taking up about 95% of the base area of my micro atx case (see pics), yet I was still able to find just enough room to stand this thing on. So it's hard to imagine a config where you couldn't make it work. Definitely recommended!

I've had this for six weeks now. I LOVE it. I can adjust to any angle I like. It's very sturdy, in fact, heavy. Which means it doesn't migrate around the desk.

The action of the keys is great. It's not overly quiet, but I like the gentle clickity clack of the keys. If you like silent typing this is not for you.

If you have a desktop computer and don't need to move your keyboard around, this keyboard is terrific.
Quite and seems durable. Move a fair amount of air. Works fine with a speed dial. Slightly better the the fans that came with my case of the same size. Would recommend.

This just makes so much sense. Hard drives are so cheap now that they can be used instead of tape for backups. And no one wants to look for external enclosures and power supplies for each one just to use a hard drive externally. Here you buy one device, leave it hooked up to your computer and just plug raw hard drives in and use them, then disconnect them when done. This is the way it should be. A+ product!!
Great display. Accurate colors, good blacks, and superb stand. Lots of built in options for adjusting the image, and a fairly complete line of presets. 1920x1200 :-)

review_title: Nice keys, font size a little horsey
review_text:
Note: I chose the Grey/Beige set. This set (YMDK 96 84 ANSI ISO Key) went on just fine, and are a great frugal find.

I bought these for an relatively inexpensive TKL mechanical wireless keyboard (RK87G) because the OEM keycaps were set in a truly fugly and illegible typeface.

These YMDKs feel good, and have a slightly deeper "thunk" when they bottom out. The two-character keys are typeset vertically, as Underwood and Remington intended. Although the font size on most of the keys is a big, they are fine and give the keyboard a bit of a homemade retro look.

NOTE Specific to the RK87G: This YMDK set does not have a ScrlLk key. The right Shift and right CTRL on this set are a little too small, so I just left the old ones on. I also left the OEM ScrlLk, Page Up, and arrow keys on because they have symbols for controlling the RGB LEDs. If you use the RKs function keys for app and control shortcuts, you may want to leave those on as well.

May 30, 2021
I've had these for a little over six months now. Still a great value set the money. I installed them on a keyboard I use for hours on end nearly every day. The printing on the beige keys hasn't faded, but I've noticed that the grey keys with white printing are beginning to fade. I'm not taking any stars off because before I purchased these I had already read other reviewers who had the same experience.

I get old laptops from friends and family when they buy new ones. I transfer their data, and sanitize the old hard disks. The ones that I keep for a while get one of the SSDs. The performance shoots up by several orders of magnitude. I've bought four or five of these, and never had a problem.

This is by far the best mouse I've ever owned, (and I've tried a lot of different makes and models). I have several, actually, one for my work computer, one each for my home computers and another one for an ASUS tablet/laptop. I also have several in "reserve" in case one fails, which doesn't happen often, if at all. Overall, a great mouse and a great value. Highly recommended.

review_title: Pleasently surprised by design and speed
review_text:
I haven't purchased a SanDisk anything for years, but after my 4mo Samsung T7 left me with a week's worth (or more I haven't discovered?) of work to redo, I read reviews and this SSD wins out.

I can only compare to the Samsung but this SanDisk runs practically cold, whereas the T7 ran quite warm. The SanDisk has a very solid feel, I wouldn't fear dropping it (though I won't, lol) whereas the T7 is so delicate and light. The cable plugs in solidly to Sandisk, whereas the T7 I'd sometimes have to wiggle to get it to recognize.

I feel pretty confident this will last me my standard couple years before replacement and I'll update if it doesn't. (And backup people! Thank goodness I had just a week before the T7 decided to willy-nilly corrupt and disappear files!)

review_title: Horribly disappointed - started corrupting files after just a couple months
review_text:
I've had many external HDDs and now SSDs, using one at a time and replacing religiously every 2-3 years even if I'm not having problems with it. WD hhds would generally go the full 3 years with no problem and then I got a Samsung T5 and loved it. At about 2.5 years it was still working superbly but I knew it needed to be replaced - my work files are too important to risk.

I bought this T7 in May and in August I opened a rarely used folder to modify some documents and they were corrupt! Not every file in the folder, just hit or miss so I thought perhaps they just hadn't copied correctly from my old drive.

But tonight -- the contents of a folder I worked on last night is corrupt! I went to work on a project I did last week and every document is not just corrupt but *GONE* from the folder.

Never again Samsung. This is horrible. As I'm copying all of the files from it to a large backup drive, the SSD is very very hot. I won't trust this brand again. I have a week of work to redo from scratch and there's no telling what else has been lost since my last backup a month ago. :(

review_title: BIG BRIGHT KEYS BUT NOISEY, CLACKITY AND HEAVY TOUCH
review_text:
Pros: Keys are large and bright; you could work on this keyboard in a cave. Wireless technology stays connected (my previous USB keyboard kept dropping the connection).

Cons: Really clunky typing. If you type fast, it will slow you down. However, if you are heavy-handed or have large fingers, you might like it (if you don't mind the noise.) The thing is clackity enough to be heard in the next room.

review_text: I have downloaded so many videos on my Mac computer that I was running out of space so I decided to move them all to an external device. I'm 75 so not exactly an up-to-date techie but I managed to format it properly by finding several good YouTube videos that helped me out. There was a sheet included with the SSD but honestly the font was so small that I could hardly read it...it took a high powered magnifier to see where I needed to go to get format instructions and even though I wrote it down carefully and re-checked the web address several times, it still did not go to the correct address for formatting instructions. Then I went to YouTube and found help. I chose SanDisk for their reputation and having used their products before, I knew they made great products. I would recommend this tiny SSD...so fast, light and a solid product. I'm glad I bought it.

Noticeably fast than my older drive.

I need more more next raid build!
Fast shipment, well described.

I originally bought this drive to use for storing large video files from family home movies. I found that, unlike other external drives, Western Digital has taken it upon themselves to make installation as lengthy and frustrating as possible, with absolutely ZERO support.

First, you can't just plug in the FireWire and have the drive work. In WinXP systems, you first have to plug in the USB cable and then have the drive autostart its own installation. Well, OK, I can see that. I did this for my laptop and it works fine. Now, here is the big problem. I wanted to transfer over a few hundred gigs of video files from my desktop's archive to the MyBook so I could edit them on my laptop...but when I plugged the USB 2.0 cable into my desktop, the drive DID NOT AUTORUN any installation software! Windows searched in vain for an appropriate driver and then couldn't install it. So I went to WD's support site and got the entire installation software package and manually installed all of them. Then I restarted and plugged in the USB cable.

NOTHING HAPPENED. The drive was unrecognizable. I tried the FireWire next, after checking in Device Management that the controlling software was OK, which it was. NOTHING. After three hours of trying to get this drive to be seen, I quit and just went out and bought a simpler drive. My [[ASIN:B0001N9VWE Apricorn 250GB EZ BUS DT HI-SPEED USB 2 ( EZ-BUS-DT-250 )]] works like a USB flash key in that it simply IDs itself as a disk drive and you can transfer files no swat. THIS THING, though, has some other mode of operation that makes it impossible to use with anything other than the first system you install it on.

WD's support is zero and their knowledge base is uninformative. I would never buy another MyBook again and I would recommend that others don't, as well, until WD increases the level and expertise of their tech support.
Learn from my mistake and use a shot of canned air to ensure that there is not any "hard" bits on the screen before using them. Do that and they should work pretty well.

Would recommend

review_title: Most silent drive I have ever owned!
review_text:
I purchased this as a data storage/backup drive for my desktop PC. My main drive is a1TB NVME drive. The data drive I use for movies, songs, and backups and digital images. Since I am not booting with the drive I don't care about raw performance, nor will I pay for it. With that said I am VERY happy with this drive. It only spins at 5400 RPM, so the access time is slightly slower, but it makes no difference to me. Maximum transfer rate is nearly 200MB/sec. High capacity drives have dense platters and are able to pull data faster.

I am a Nazi for eliminating extraneous sound and used to keep my drives inside enclosures to reduce sound. My quietest drive to date is the Samsung HD 503HI, and this is even quieter. I have several large case fans spinning slowly and if I turn them off I can ever so slightly hear a faint humming or click, but otherwise I hear NOTHING.

This is my first WD drive (have always used Samsung). I cannot speak to the drive's reliability as I've only had it for one month. It is labeled for "Surveillance," so if it's meant to be running 24/7- 365 it is meant to get use in commercial/industrial environments.

I think everyone with a desktop PC should adopt this system. It is very easy to backup anything important- save it to your C: drive as well as your backup E: drive or whatever. If one your main drive goes kaput you have the backup to pull your saved data from. You can use flash drives for additional redundancy and portability, but in my experience they are not so reliable.

I have this decent entry level gamer box that has a large HDD. So, the drive is the bottleneck. Unfortunately, the motherboard on this ACER box only has ONE sata connector. It appears the DVD drive uses a different interface (???), so luckily, it does have an M2 slot. (though not a NVMe supporting one)
It's been installed now for about 4 months and the systems is faster, more responsive and games load much faster. Boot time is seconds instead of up to a minute.

The price is a bit high, however compared to a regular SSD.

I wanted something a bit more compact and slicker than your typical clunky black Logitech keyboards. I also wanted something that had a mouse that shared the reciever usb dongle. This was affordable and so I took a chance.
It is a lower and flatter profile for both the keyboards and the mouse, I am sure you could get a pad to make it more ergonomic.. but so far it isn't too bad.
I like the softness of the keys AND an added bonus is that it comes with a silicone? cover that you lay over the keys to keep dust and food out of them! PLus

The keyboard layout isn't totally standard and it is missing some bells and whistles but nothing that I think is going to be too difficult. We will see.

I like how light it is, and the silver color is a nice change. So many computer peripherals are just black black black and while that may be ok to some degree, it is nice to have a bit of color.

overall like it.

review_title: Quality that even a cheapskate can love
review_text:

I often read in bed in the dark and love the way the cover works here. At some angles there's a bit of a flare of light on the screen closest to the light, but a little adjustment fixes that. It's tens times easier than wrestling with a paperbound book and an attached book light.

I find that I take my Kindle out of the cover fairly often to play games or do anything much with the key pad. The first day or so I scared myself by not lining it up quite properly and having the top hinge engaged while the bottom one was only part of the way hooked in. I just patiently and gently worked it till the top hinge disengaged and made a mental note to pay a little attention when I slip the Kindle onto the hinges.

Great product.
Easy to connect, sound quality is good...overall, it's nice but kind of plain for my taste.

review_title: Great field of view and picture, poor audio.
review_text:
[[VIDEOID:ee16abd42051bd8086d9f1506e278779]] The good: Clear picture, useful zoom, very versatile set-up. I love the included tripod especially, it makes it very easy to set up and place. I wrapped it around an old tripod that was missing its head to make a 90-degree rig for my art. The movement is excellent, and the broader field of view gives it some more uses over traditional webcams. It really is plug-and-play. I had no issues getting the computer to recognize it.

The bad: The audio leaves a lot to be desired. It is tinny and doesn’t pick up well if you turn away from the camera. The remote also is extremely sensitive to where it is angled.

I plan to use it to record art time-lapses of painting and sketching. I can also see using it for running a tabletop role-playing game where some folks are remote to capture more of the table than a traditional webcam. I have a PC, and the included video was recorded in the native Camera app for Windows.

I headlined this review "Linux loads fine," but with a caveat: neither Debian or Ubuntu detected the onboard wifi card. No prob. I have a USB wifi dongle that plays well with Linux and used that to test the installs.

One of the first things I did was pull the included 128gb NVMe (which is preloaded with Windows) and replaced it with another NVMe stick I had on hand. Then I installed an SSD in the 2.5-inch SATA drive bay. Getting to the SSD bay is easy. You just remove a single Phillips screw and slide a lock switch to the side and the top lifts off the box. Getting to the NVMe socket (which I'd guess most people are probably unlikely to need to do) is another matter. It requires loosening the main board by removing four screws that are accessed by pulling off the rubber bottom corner pads. A magnetic screwdriver comes in really handy, especially during reassembly.

The system didn't detect the replacement NVMe stick I installed. Maybe a compatibility issue, or the original stick is proprietary in the BIOS or something, not a machine flaw. It did detect the SATA connected SSD, so I went ahead. The BIOS had no prob booting from a USB stick. Installation of both Debian and Ubuntu went without a hitch, except for the wifi card issue I mentioned. That's not unusual when installing Linux in machines with recent-generation wifi cards. Sometimes the drivers just aren't available.

The bottom line for me is this mini PC is capable, runs smoothly, graphics look good (but don't expect to run this as a gaming machine), and it is pretty quiet. And Linux will load on it. It would make an excellent Linux-based file server or media server with a hard-wired Ethernet connection. If you just go with the Windows OS and NVMe stick it comes with, it all works right out of the box, and you can add a SATA 2.5 inch SSD for more storage.

review_title: Love everything but the integrated wrist rest
review_text:
I love the layout of this keyboard. I love that it is tenkeyless. I love the action of the keys. It's a membrane keyboard, not a mechanical, but the keys operate smoothly with a relatively light touch. It's pretty quiet. The whole keyboard, though plastic, has a good durable feel.

The only thing I don't like is the built-in wrist rest. It slopes down too steeply to actually give any elevation to wrist position. It's smooth plastic and has no padding. And the keyboard does not come with a front edge riser, only back edge folding supports. I'm using it with improvised front edge elevation and wearable wrist rests. But I like everything else about this keyboard so I may keep using it.

First let me tell you what I like about this keyboard: I like the key action. Keys have a decently long stroke and are easy to press and don't feel spongy. I like the split layout, which makes for a much more natural position for the arms. I like the split spacebar. To me, these are advantages over the Logitech K350 I've been using, which has a curved, not split, key layout and a spongy feel when typing.

What I don't like, and what was pretty much a dealbreaker to me (I thought about returning it almost immediately) is the "wrist rest." It is short and rolls off steeply and provides no wrist support at all, unless you like typing with your wrist positioned lower than your knuckles and your hands bent upwards from the wrist. The recommended position is wrist level with the knuckles, which is called the "neutral" position. I personally prefer typing with my wrists positioned slightly higher than my knuckles.

Look at the product photos and notice that the typist doesn't even have his wrist on the wrist rest. He or she is using a hover hand technique, I guess to make things look more ergonomic or something, because if their wrists were actually on the wrist rest, their hands would be obviously bent upwards at the wrists to reach the keys.

I'm at a loss as to why many keyboard manufacturers (including Logitech with the K350) provide legs to raise the back of the keyboard and don't provide anything to raise the front. That just makes the "backwards" bend at the wrist even more pronounced.

This Periboard keyboard is no exception to that. It has foldaway legs at the back and none in the front. But even if it had legs to raise the front, it wouldn't provide much improvement. I raised the front a couple of inches with a foam wedge I use for keyboard support, and the wrist rest was still so low I pressed the spacebar when reaching for the F2 key.

I even tried adding foam wrist rests but the built-in rest is so steep and short it actually interferes with using a really functional rest. I even tried using wearable wrist rests---which are kind of annoying on their own since they aren't all that stable---and the steep slope and short length of the built-in wrist rest made that a less than effective solution. This keyboard might have been a lot better if it had no built-in wrist rest at all. That way you could use your own and set it up just like you like it.

It's disappointing, actually. I like the key action and layout, but the wrist rest pretty much nerfs the whole thing. I may keep it and experiment with solutions from time to time. I might even see if I can cut off the built-in rest and replace it with something made of wood or something, or just get it out of the way so I can use some other effective wrist rest.

In the meantime, I'm probably going to stick with the spongy-action, non-split Logitech K350. In fact I'm typing this review on it, though I would have liked to use the Periboard 512. But until I come up with a better wrist rest solution it's just easier to use the K350.

And a couple more quick points, comparing this keyboard to the K350, this keyboard is wired while the K350 is wireless. The overall footprint of both (length and width) is almost the same. I personally don't use or need the multimedia keys on either.

Because of the better key action and, to me, better key layout, if it had a better wrist rest, or none at all, this Periboard 512 might have become my go-to keyboard.

review_title: Pixel density is where it's at!
review_text:
Pixels per inch is where it's at!

I bought the 24" 1440 model for one reason: Pixel density.

I'm not a gamer. For me it's all about legible screen fonts for easy reading. And pixels per inch is where it's at. The higher the pixel density, the clearer the type looks. Fonts on a larger monitor with a lower density won't look as clear as a smaller one with a higher number of pixels per inch.

The density on the 24" model (2560 x 1440 resolution) is a little over 120 pixels per inch (ppi). A Kindle Paperwhite pixel density is 300 ppi. So if this monitor is a bit over twice the distance from you as a Kindle Paperwhite, the density and clarity will look about the same.

There is one thing I do want to mention: brightness. Wow this thing is bright. In the early days of LCD and LED monitors, brightness and color accuracy were issues. The brightness issue has certainly been solved, and maybe too well. I have mine set on just "5" on the on-board brightness setting. Occasionally I have dialed it down to "0" and it's still readable.

Truly plug and play. Simple 3-cable setup (plus a power cable). Windows 8.1 recognized it instantly, didn't even have to install drivers. Works immediately with Google Hangouts, Skype, and all the conferencing apps we tried.

The instructions are simple and clear. The only real critical piece of information you need from the setup manual is to not attempt to physically move the camera around by hand -- just use the remote control to move it.

The picture quality is impressive. The camera is large and very high quality, obviously has a great sensor. It's tolerant of high contrast environments. We tested it in a backlit environment and faces were still highly visible.

It's HD capable (up to 1080P), it zooms 10:1 by remote control for closeups, shows whiteboards beautifully and in sharp detail, pulls back to a very wide view (we were able to see both corners of a 12-foot-wide wall from only 8 feet away, so it easily would show participants at a conference table), and all camera movements are simple from the remote. Just by pressing one button a few seconds you can easily program a "home" position so the camera can automatically swing back to a main speaker every time you push the button again.

The audio is amazing too. Even standing several feet from the base unit, the person speaking sounds like they are wired with a personal, close mic. This is due to some pretty sophisticated noise-cancelling technology. Room echo is practically eliminated.

Which also makes the speakerphone quality great too. You can hear remote participants very clearly.

I know this thing is built for small business use, but I could see this as a great home use system for online family or friend get-togethers when some friends or family are scattered around the globe. And it would make a superb personal webcam, particularly if you want to be able to pan and zoom in on things around a room or shop and show them in HD detail.

The only minor gripe I can think of is that the camera swivels to a to a down-and-side position when it turns off. A good position -- people won't get uncomfortable seeing a camera pointed at them, and the lens is protected. But is not the position it was packaged in, and you aren't supposed to force it manually, so it won't fit back in the original box for storage.

As I said, that's a minor gripe. Everything else about this system is five star all the way.

This review is for the 157 Key Sortie keycap set.

The profile is ZDA, which the maker says is similar to XDA but higher. The keycaps are ⅜ of an inch tall. I do think the ZDA profile is high.

This is a review for the Kiwi Switch from DAIDAI AJAZZ. The Kiwi switch is tactile, 50gf, and housed in glittery translucent green. If you have clear keycaps, you can see the yellow stem and a little of the upper housing.

For the Kiwi switches, you get 46 switches. For most keyboards, 46 switches is not enough and you will need 2-3 cans.

The switches come in a clear plastic can, with a screw lid and a pull tab. The packaging is cute! More importantly, the can takes up less space than the usual plastic tray, and it’s reusable.

I use Akko Vintage Whites (linear), but I wanted to try tactile switches for the thumb clusters on my ergo keyboard, so I had feedback when I pressed those keys. The tactile bump is smooth and pronounced, I definitely know I pressed that key.

I didn’t notice any difference between these pre-lubed Kiwi switches and non-lubed switches.

review_title: No tactile bumps on F and J, amazing for backlighting
review_text:
I have the “White” color option in this set of keycaps from Akko. White is a bit misleading, the color is actually glossy and nearly translucent. This is actually what I wanted, I was looking all over for nearly clear keycaps, but I did want to point that out.

If you like maximum backlighting, this might be the set for you. I was using white pudding caps before, and I thought they let a lot of light shine through. The difference is night and day. These Akko caps show backlighting on all sides and the top of the cap. I’ve included a picture of a white pudding cap surrounded by the clear Akkos to show the difference.

I’m using the keycaps with Akko Vintage White (MX) switches. The keycaps fit well, but they took a bit of force to fit on the switches.

I am disappointed the F and J keys do not have ridges or bumps. I’m a touch typist and using an ergo board with 56 keys, I rely on those ridges to help me orient my hands. This set has so much variety that I wish Akko had included doubles of F and J or even blanks with the ridges.

Speaking of keycap variety: the set has some great 1u options! My current keyboard is an Iris Rev 6, all keys are 1u size. But most keycap sets don’t have 1u keycaps for Shift, Control, Command/Windows, and so on. This set does, which is a big help. I also like the cute animal keycaps, they add some fun to my board.

I believe the ASA height is original to Akko. They have a helpful height chart on their site, comparing ASA to OEM, JDA, OSA, and Cherry. I was using OEM before, and switching to ASA and the glossy feel of the keycaps took about two days of adjustment.

The Leadsail Rechargeable Wireless Mouse is a basic mouse. The sort I’d toss into a backpack for when I’m on the go, or use as a backup.

This isn’t a mouse I would use on a daily basis -- it’s not comfortable in my hand for long term use. The mouse feels short in my hand, and I have small hands. My pinky finger falls off the side, so my finger aches after a while.

I do like that the mouse has a curved top, so it sort of nestles into my palm. It’s not truly ergonomic, but I’ve tried other similar mouses that are flat, so I noticed a difference.

I tried the mouse on my Mac laptop, which recognized it immediately. The left and right click buttons are almost silent.

The best thing about this mouse is that it’s rechargeable -- no having to worry about batteries. And the USB receiver fits into the bottom of the mouse, reducing the chance of losing it.

review_title: The ONLY hard drive I have ever trusted . . . WD Elements Portable External Hard Drive
review_text:
09/09/2020 update:
Last 2 4T harddrives that I have purchased from Amazon have been defective. The male end of the cord would not seamlessly fit into the female portion of the hard drive. Both returned. I am purchased directly from WD from this point forward. BE VERY CAREFUL. IF CORD DOES NOT FIT SEAMLESSLY and the female end is not lining up perfectly for the male end . . . DO NOT USE IT AND RETURN!

8/15/2020:
In 15 years, I have had 2 laptops crash. And 1 desktop crash in that amount of time. But - I have never lost information. I don't store my information on my desktop or laptop . . . I worked solely off of harddrives. I have used the WD Elements Hard Drives for over 15 years now. I had 1 4tb that I used over and over again to back up my laptop and personal files. As I got busier with work and life . . . fast forward 15 years and I now have 6 of these. I work daily off of 2 of these . . . one has personal files and the other has work files. No delay. That being said . . . my desktop has a top of the line processor, but I don't think that works to make the hard drive move any faster. But still . . . I work all day every day without any delays . . .

I have 2 backups of the original working harddrives - for work and for personal. I back up every single week like clockwork.

I then have 2 backups of the 1st backups. You don't want to be backing up your working harddrive (thereby putting into play your original harddrive and your 1st back up harddrive) . . . so you need a 2nd back up in the event something catastrophic occurs during the back up of your original harddrives. So I have 3 each for work (1 I work off of every day) and 3 each for personal (1 I work off of every day).

I know that I will always have a full set of my work files, my Outlook files and my accounting files.

Yep . . . it's a $600 investment for peace of mind and security of my files . . . and it's a system that works for me . . .

I have used other harddrives by WD and I personally don't care for them. I especially dislike the wifi / icloud ones. These elements are so easy . . . just plug it in and go. Or in my case . . . plug them in and work all day every day.

I was in the market for a case for a thin mini itx system I was building and this one was the cheapest I came across that didn't make me fear for my components. I read all the reviews I could find and even watched a few YouTube videos and ultimately decided that this was the case for me. The build went fairly smoothly (no late night trips to find parts I found out I needed at the last minute or incompatibility issues), but I did encounter a few problems which other reviewers had also mentioned and I chose to ignore.

First Problem: Cannot use hdd mount with stock Intel heat sink installed
The product description claims this case can accommodate a stock heatsink, which is absolutely true, but if you do use one, a hard drive, even a thin ssd like I used, can't be mounted using the bracket they provided. I thought I was stuck at this point, and even tried mounting the ssd to the top of the case, but then I noticed some screw holes on the back of the case just above the I/O shield that seemed to be spaced just right for the holes on the side of the ssd. A few minutes and a little creative drill work later, and I had a place to mount my ssd, no bracket required.

Second Problem: The front panel connectors are way too short
My major problem with this case is the front panel connectors. For a case this small, it seems like it would be easy to include cables long enough to reach from the corner where they connect to the case to the opposite corner, just to be sure there was enough wire no matter what the motherboard setup was. Minibox did not take this approach, leaving me to splice the wires for the power button with and led with doorbell wire and plug the front two usb connector into a single auxiliary usb header, which only allows one port to work. It's mainly for this reason that I knocked off a star.

In conclusion, this is a really nice, well-made case if you're willing to deal with the few problems that it has. View the attached pictures for a better idea of how I ended up mounting the ssd and a general view of what this case looks like with a system in it.
